bio.en: Nir Eyal is the author of the bestselling books Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products and Indistractable: How to Control Your Attention, and a teacher and consultant at the intersection of psychology, technology, and business.
bio.zh: Nir Eyal 是畅销书《钩住：如何打造让人上瘾的产品》（Hooked）与《不可分心：如何掌控你的注意力》（Indistractable）的作者，也是一位游走于心理学、科技与商业交叉领域的导师与顾问。

summary.en: Nir explains that distraction is not a character flaw but a failure to plan, and introduces a four-step model - master internal triggers, make time for traction, hack back external triggers, and prevent distractions with pacts - to become indistractable. He stresses that the root cause of distraction is often our attempt to escape discomfort, and that scheduling values-based time weekly is more effective than reactive to-do lists. The conversation is packed with practical tactics for regaining focus and doing the work that matters.
summary.zh: Nir 指出，分心不是性格缺陷，而是缺乏规划的结果，并提出了四步模型来变得“不可分心”：掌控内在诱因、为“专注”预留时间、回击外部干扰、用约定（pact）防止分心。他强调，分心的根源往往是我们逃避不适感，而每周基于价值观安排时间，比被动的待办清单更有效。本期充满了重新夺回注意力、去做真正重要之事的实用技巧。

(00:00:51): It's not the pings, dings, and rings. It's the feelings. But to me, that's incredibly empowering because once you realize, "Wait a minute, it's just a feeling." We already know these things. What we don't know is how to get out of our own way, how to stop getting distracted. And so, that was certainly my problem. And so, what I wanted to do was really dive into the problem because the conventional solutions didn't work for me. When I have a problem in my life, I'll think about it, I'll write about it, I'll talk to friends, I'll talk to my wife about it. If I still can't figure it out, I'll read books about it. And what the conventional wisdom out there written by a lot of college professors that are all tenured is stop using technology, stop checking email, get off social media. It's melting your brain, but that's not very helpful, right? (00:07:23): Maybe if you have tenure, that's okay, but I can't stop using technology. My career will plummet. I have to use these tools. So, where do we begin? Maybe the best place to start is by first, before we dive into the tactics around how do we become indistractable, the first place to start is what is distraction? Understanding the term really, really matters. And the best way to understand what distraction is, is to understand what distraction is not. What's the opposite of distraction? So, if you ask most people, what's the opposite of distraction? (00:08:06): They'll tell you focus, right? I don't want to be distracted, I want to be focused. That's not exactly right. Then in fact, the opposite of distraction is not focus. The opposite of distraction is traction. Becomes pretty easy when you look at both words, traction, distraction. They're opposites because both words come from the same Latin root, trahare, which means to pull, and they both end in the same six letters, A-C-T-I-O-N that spells action, reminding us that distraction is not something that happens to us. It is an action that we ourselves take. So, traction, by definition, is any action that pulls you towards what you say you were going to do, things you do with intent, things that move you closer to your values, and help you become the kind of person you want to become. Those are acts of traction. Now, the opposite of traction, distraction, is any action that pulls you away from what you plan to do, further away from your goals, further away from becoming the kind of person you want to become. (00:09:01): And what separates traction from distraction is one word, and that one word is intent. I love this Dorothy Parker. She said, "The time you plan to waste is not wasted time." So, I think we need to stop medicalizing and moralizing what people do with their time. Why is it that someone going on Reddit or on social media or watching a YouTube video that's somehow morally inferior to watching a football game on TV? It's not. Anything you want to do with your time and attention is fine as long as it's done with intent, as long as you're doing it on your schedule, and not someone else's, certainly not the tech company's schedule. So, anything you do with intent is traction, anything else is distraction. So, what I discovered, for me, was that I was getting tricked by distraction in that the most pernicious form of distraction I discovered was the kind I didn't even realize was distracting me. (00:09:53): So, let me know if this sounds familiar to you, Lenny. I would sit down at my desk. I would look at my to-do list. By the way, we can talk about why to-do lists are one of the worst things you can do for your personal productivity. We can get back to that later. But I would sit down at my desk and I'd say, "Okay, I've got that big important project. That's what I'm going to do this morning. I'm not going to get distracted, nothing's going to get in my way. turns.zh:
好的，这里有更深层的动机。就像是“我需要帮助”，这很棒。我最喜欢做的事，就是和人们具体探讨他们面临的挑战。但让我先回顾一下。我花了五年时间写一本书，就是因为什么？因为我太容易分心了。所以，我写这本书更多是为了自己，而不是为了别人。正是我写书的唯一原因。不是因为我知道什么，而是因为我想知道什么。我发现自己有太多误区、陈词滥调，甚至是直接有害的行为，这些都阻碍了我的生产力。当我真正回归到第一性原理，研究相关文献时，发现自己做错了太多事。

（00:05:56）但自从我改变了方法，采用研究文献提出的应对分心策略后，生活发生了难以置信的改善。45岁的我状态最佳，与家人关系比以往更亲密，工作效率远超往昔。这并非因为我不知道该怎么做。我发现如今人们面临的真正问题，不是不知道该怎么做。过去可能是祖父母那代人，信息匮乏，只能去图书馆查资料。如今有互联网，基本都知道该怎么做。若不知道，就谷歌搜索。但我们都清楚基本常识，比如想健身就得锻炼和合理饮食，对吧？（00:06:38）这没必要看减肥书。想和家人建立良好关系，就全身心陪伴他们。想在工作中更出色，就承担别人不愿做的苦差事。我们都知道这些道理，却不知道如何摆脱自身的束缚，如何停止分心。这确实是我的问题所在。

我决定深入研究这个问题，因为传统解决方案对我无效。当生活中遇到难题，我会思考、写作、与朋友交流、与妻子探讨。若仍无法解决，就阅读相关书籍。主流观点由终身教职的大学教授主导：别用科技产品、别查邮件、别刷社交媒体。这些建议没用，对吧？（00:07:23）或许对有终身教职的人适用，但我离不开科技，否则事业会一落千丈。所以我需要更实用的方法。研究发现：分心的根源比停止使用科技更耐人寻味，解决方案也远比“科技有害、会毁脑”更有力量。那么从何入手？或许最重要的第一步，是在深入探讨如何变得不易分心之前，先理解什么是分心。理解分心的最佳途径，是先理解分心不是什么。分心的反面是什么？当问大多数人分心的反面是什么？（00:08:06）他们会说“专注”，但这并不准确。分心的反面不是专注，而是……
分心的反面是专注。看看这两个词——“traction”和“distraction”，你会发现它们是反义词。这是因为它们都源自同一个拉丁词根“trahare”，意思是“拉”，且结尾字母相同，拼成“action”，提醒我们分心并非被动发生，而是我们主动选择的结果。因此，专注的定义是任何能将你引向既定目标的行动——那些带着意图去做的事，能让你更贴近价值观，帮助你成为理想中的自己。这就是专注的行为。

与此相对，分心则是将你引向相反方向的行动——偏离目标，背离理想。（00:09:01）区分两者的关键词是“意图”。我很欣赏多萝西·帕克的名言：“你打算浪费的时间，绝非真正浪费。” 我们不应将人们如何支配时间归为道德问题——为何浏览Reddit、社交媒体或观看YouTube视频就比看电视足球赛低人一等？其实不然。只要带着意图利用时间，只要遵循自己的节奏而非他人的安排（尤其是科技公司的日程表），任何行为都是专注的体现，余者皆为分心。

我发现自己常被分心所困，最致命的分心形式往往是最不易察觉的。（00:09:53）你或许感同身受：我曾坐在书桌前，翻阅待办清单（顺便说一句，待办清单是个人生产力的最大杀手，这个话题可以深入探讨）。明明决心专注于重要项目，却总先打开邮箱看看有没有新邮件。

So, you asked a big question, I gave you a big answer. That's the overall framework. That's a strategy. Tactics are what you do. Strategy is why you do it. So, I wanted to explain the strategy before we got into the tactics.
turns.zh: 这完全是自传式的。这就是我过去常做的事……“哦，让我再看看那个Slack频道。办公室里大家都在干什么？哦，让我再看看行业新闻。”这很重要。这是我的工作职责之一。我在提高效率，对吧？但我没意识到，分心会让我优先处理紧急且简单的事务，而忽略了推进生活和事业所需的艰难而重要的工作。所以，仅仅因为这是一项与工作相关的任务，并不意味着它就不是分心了。事实上，这才是最糟糕的分心方式。远比玩《糖果粉碎传奇》之类的游戏更糟糕，因为后者至少能让你明显意识到自己在分心。但如果你只是在查看工作邮件，尽管这也是分心行为，却会让你觉得自己在高效工作，因为这不符合你预先设定的时间和注意力分配方式。所以现在，我们有了这个框架。我们有“专注力”和“分心因素”。（00:11:08）：现在，还有一件超级重要的事，之后我们就能把整个局面理清楚，这样我们就能不再纠结于模型，而是真正着手去做事了。既然我们有了“专注力”和“分心因素”这两个概念，我们还需要考虑“触发因素”。触发因素分为两种：外部触发因素和内部触发因素。外部触发因素就是我们外部环境中的那些常见因素，比如提示音、通知、手机震动等，我们往往把这些归咎于分心，但研究发现，这些只占我们分心的10%原因。那么剩下的90%呢？结果发现，90%时候的分心并非源于外部环境，而是大多数分心始于内部——无聊、孤独、疲惫、不确定性、焦虑。这些才是我们90%分心的根源。所以，无论是过多的新闻、过多的酒、过多的足球、过多的Facebook，除非你理解问题的根源，否则你总会被这样或那样的事情分心。（00:12:09）：所以，成为不受分心影响的第一步，是掌控这些内部触发因素，否则它们就会反过来控制你。我们围绕这四点展开。第二步，为专注力腾出时间。我们可以谈谈这个。抵御外部触发因素，第四步，用协议防止分心。所以，你问了一个大问题，我给了一个大答案。这就是整体框架。这是一项策略。战术是你的行动。策略是你的行动依据。所以，在深入战术之前，我想先解释一下策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I love this word traction because it relates to kind of the other side of this podcast of growth, product market fit, building products people want, getting traction with users. So, I really like that there's this additional way of thinking about traction, which is basically not being distracted. Can you just repeat the four steps again for people to have this in mind?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我喜欢“专注力”这个词，因为它与这个播客中关于成长、产品市场匹配、打造用户想要的产品、获得用户牵引力的另一面息息相关。所以，我很高兴能有这样一种额外思考专注力的方式，基本上就是不被分心。你能不能再把这四个步骤重复一遍，让大家记住？

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Step number one, master internal triggers. Step number two, make time for traction. So, this is where we're turning our values into time. We can talk about how to do that. Step number three is hack back the external triggers. This is where we get into the pings, dings, and rings, not just the obvious stuff like your phone, your computer. I take about a page and a half to talk about that. That's kind of kindergarten stuff. But what about all the non-obvious external triggers? What about stupid meetings that didn't need to be called? What about emails that didn't need to be sent and received? What about our kids? Our kids are wonderful. I know you're a new dad, they're fantastic to have kids, but they can also be a source of distraction. So, how do we deal with all those external triggers, and then finally prevent distraction with pacts and pacts are this firewall, this last resort against distraction that we can use to keep distraction at bay and it's really about these four steps in concert in this order that anyone can use to become indistractable.
turns.zh: 步骤一，掌控内在触发因素。步骤二，为专注力留出时间。这就是我们如何将价值观转化为时间的问题。我们可以探讨如何做到这一点。步骤三，规避外部触发因素。这里我们要应对各种提示、通知和提醒声，不只是手机和电脑之类的显而易见的干扰源。我用了大约一页半的篇幅来讲解这些内容——这算是基础知识。但那些不那么显眼的外部触发因素呢？比如那些本不该召开的无意义会议？那些本不必发送和接收的邮件？还有我们的孩子？孩子固然可爱，但他们也可能成为分心的源头。所以，如何应对这些外部触发因素，最后通过契约来抵御干扰，这才是真正关键的四步组合，任何人都能借此变得专注不受干扰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Does this spell something clever, by the way?
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺便说一句，这拼写得挺巧妙的，对吧？

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: No, I didn't have an acronym, but I do have a pretty picture.
turns.zh: 不，我没想用什么缩写，但我倒是有张漂亮的图片。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So, let's go through this and I'd love specifically example you shared, I think many people run into this. There's a hard thing I need to do and I'm just going to go check my email and Twitter instead. I feel like that's a very common distraction, and so sharing, getting into that at some point would be awesome, but otherwise let's get into these four steps.
turns.zh: 太棒了。那我们来逐一分析吧。我特别想听听你分享的具体例子，我觉得很多人都会遇到这种情况。有件重要的事要做，结果却去查看邮箱和推特了。我觉得这是很常见的分心行为，所以能分享一下相关经历就太好了。但先来讲讲这四个步骤。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Yeah, well, we can absolutely do that. So, is that something you encounter? It sounds like a...
turns.zh: 好的，你确实遇到过这种情况吧？听起来你……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 100%. Every time. I have my to-do list, work on next week's post, and then I'm like, "Oh, let me just go check Twitter or maybe tweet something and that'll be fun," and then totally check my email. "Oh, inbox zero. Let's get all the way to zero. Oh, that's cool. Okay, now the days are over."
turns.zh: 百分百每次都这样。我列好待办清单，准备写下周的博文，然后就想：“哦，先去看看推特吧，或者发条动态也挺有趣的。”接着就完全沉浸在邮箱里了。“哦，收件箱清空了。那就彻底清空吧。真不错。好吧，一天就这么过去了。”

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Exactly. And by the way, we are cut from the same cloth. This is exactly the pattern I used to get into and I knew I wasn't doing my best because I wasn't putting in the time to the things that were most important. I was doing just what was easy and what was urgent and that's not good enough. So, if we use this model, step number one is master the internal triggers. So, for you, Lenny, so when you say, "Okay, I know I've got to do this big important thing, but now I'm going to go check email," I would guess that there's some kind of underlying emotion that you're trying to escape. Let's put yourself in the shoes that you were in when you said, "I was going to do that big important thing, but now I'm going to check email instead." Do you remember the last time that happened, by the way?
turns.zh: 没错。说真的，我们真是同病相怜。这正是我过去常陷入的怪圈。我知道自己没能全力以赴，是因为没有把时间投入到最重要的事情上。我只做那些简单易行、紧急又紧迫的事，但这远远不够。所以，如果我们遵循这个模式，第一步就是掌控内在触发因素。对你来说，伦尼，当你说“好吧，我知道自己该做这件重要的事，但现在我要去查邮箱”时，我猜你内心深处是想逃避某种情绪。让我们设身处地想想你当时的处境：你本打算做那件重要的事，却最后去查邮箱了。你还记得上次这样的时候吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Every morning.
turns.zh: 每天早上。

turns.en: Every morning. This morning?
turns.zh: 每天早上。这次呢？

turns.zh: 好的，完美。你还记得在转去查邮箱或发推特之前，内心深处在逃避什么？还是说你本该做的事？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if this is an emotion or feeling, but there's just this, I need to get serious and start using my brain and there's going to be this deep work moment where I just get real deep and it takes a lot of effort to push me into that. Sometimes easier, sometimes harder. So, maybe it's avoiding this, "Oh, okay, I'm going to really have to think." It's like, I guess, it's the fear of the brain starting to really have to work.
turns.zh: 我不知道这是一种情绪还是感觉，但就是这样，我需要认真起来，开始动脑筋，然后就会有那种深度工作的时刻——我会深挖下去，但这需要耗费大量精力。有时容易些，有时难些。所以，也许这是在逃避，"哦，好吧，我真的得好好思考了。"就像，我猜，这是一种对大脑开始真正运转的恐惧。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Yeah, that's hard work. So maybe, it's a bit of laziness. Maybe, it's a bit of momentum. There's this uncomfortable feeling of this cold start problem. "Oh, I don't really want to do it right now." So, this is incredibly important and I appreciate your candor here around what you feel because all of us experience it and we don't want to talk about it. We want to think that it's, "Oh, I'll just grayscale my phone," or, "I'll just turn off notifications and that's going to solve the problem," and it never does. And let me tell you, I tried all of it. I went to Alibaba and I bought myself one of these flip phones from China like we used to have in the 1990s with no apps, no internet connection, and then I got myself a word processor off of eBay, so that I could just sit down and write and do the important stuff. (00:16:33): And even when I stopped using all the technology, even when I got rid of all the apps, I would sit down on my desk and I'd say, "Oh, you know what? There's that book that I've been meaning what to do some research in," or, "Let me just clean off my desk real quick," or, "You know what? I should take out the trash." And I kept getting distracted because the problem is not our technology. The problem is our inability to deal with discomfort. So, what I have adopted for myself and what I'd advise anyone who finds themselves in this situation is to always identify what is that internal trigger, what is that itch that you are looking to escape when you get distracted, because that is the source of 90% of our distractions. It's not the pings, dings, and rings. It's the feelings. But to me, that's incredibly empowering because once you realize, "Wait a minute, it's just a feeling." It's all it is, it's just an emotion. Then you can have tools ready to go. You can have arrows in your quiver ready to take out as soon as you feel that discomfort. (00:17:27): So, let me give you one tool that I use every single day. Feel free to use it next time you feel this same problem. It's called the 10-minute rule, and this is just one of a dozen different techniques that you can use that I put in the book, but this is one that I use almost every single day. So, for me, I've been a professional writer now for over a decade, and writing is never easy. I hear people say like, "Oh, just form a writing habit." I think that's ridiculous. I don't know what they're talking about. A habit is defined as a behavior done with little or no conscious thought. I don't know how to write out of habit. Writing is always hard. Fricking work. I've written two bestsellers, thousands of articles and let me tell you, it's always difficult. It's hard, and all I want to do when I write is just Google this one thing or let me just check the news real quick or let me just do anything but the actual writing. So, here's what I do.
turns.zh:
是啊，这确实很费力。所以也许，这有点懒惰。也许，这有点被动力。有种不适感，就像遇到"冷启动问题"。"哦，我现在真的不想做这件事。"所以，这件事非常重要，我很感激你能坦诚地谈论自己的感受，因为我们都经历过这种情况，却不愿谈论它。我们总想说"哦，我只要把手机调成灰度模式"，或者"只要关掉通知就行了"，但这根本不管用。让我告诉你，我试过所有这些方法。我去阿里巴巴买了一部像90年代我们用的那种没有应用程序、没有网络连接的翻盖手机，然后在eBay上买了一个文字处理器，这样我就能坐下来写作，处理重要的事情。（00:16:33）：即使我停止使用所有科技产品，卸载了所有应用程序，我也会坐在书桌前，说："哦，你知道吗？有一本书我一直想查些资料的，"或者"让我快速清理一下书桌吧，"或者"你知道吗？我该去倒垃圾了。"然后我总是分心，因为问题不在于我们的科技产品。问题在于我们无法应对不适感。所以，我为自己采用的策略，也是我建议任何陷入这种情况的人采取的策略，就是始终识别出那个内在的触发因素，那个你想逃避以避免分心的痒处，因为这就是我们90%分心的根源。不是提示音、通知和铃声，而是那些情绪。但对我来说，这非常有力量，因为一旦你意识到，"等一下，这只是种感觉。"仅此而已，只是一种情绪。然后你就可以准备好应对工具了。你可以把箭装进你的箭袋，一旦感觉到不适就立刻拿出来用。
（00:17:27）：所以，让我给你一个我每天都在用的工具。下次遇到同样的问题时，随时可以用。这叫做"10分钟规则"，这只是我在书中提到的十几种技巧之一，但这是我几乎每天都会用的一个工具。对我来说，我做职业作家已经十多年了，写作从来都不容易。我听到人们说"哦，养成写作习惯就行了。"我觉得这太荒谬了。我不知道他们在说什么。习惯被定义为几乎不需要或不需要有意识思考的行为。我不知道怎么能凭习惯写作。写作总是很费力。真是他妈的累人。我写了两本畅销书，几千篇文章，让我告诉你，这一直很困难。很困难，写作时我总想谷歌一下这个东西，或者快速看看新闻，或者做任何事，就是不写作。所以，以下是我会做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By the way, there's a great quote that I'll share real quick about this that I think I share often on this podcast that I think it's falsely attributed to Hemingway, but it's that, "Writing is easy. Just sit down at the keyboard and bleed."
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，关于这个话题我还有一句很棒的引语，我想我经常在播客里分享这句话。不过据说这句话是被错误地归于海明威的，但原意是：“写作很简单。只要坐在键盘前，倾注真心就行了。”

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Oh my God, that's so true. It's so true, and I've not figured out how to make it suddenly easy. Every single word is hard to type out, but I got to do it right and I love doing it. I love having done it. In the process, it's very difficult. But after I make the discovery, after I create something that I think is useful, then it's a lot of fun. But doing the work is really difficult. So, here's what I do. Every time that I am tempted to go do something else, which is all the time, what I will do is I will take out a timer, I'll take out my phone and I'll say, "Set a timer for 10 minutes." I'll put the phone down and my job is for those 10 minutes, whenever I'm ready, get back to the task at hand or do what's called surf the urge. (00:19:12): Surfing the urge acknowledges that these emotions are like waves. They crest and then they subside. But that's not how we think about emotions. Most of us think about emotions as always being there. If I feel bored, I feel like I'm always going to be bored. If I'm frustrated, it feels like I'm always going to be frustrated, but that's never the case. Emotions are like waves. So, your job is to set that timer for 10 minutes and realize you can do just about anything for just 10 minutes. So, the idea is not to say don't do it. We know that this technique that a lot of people use of abstinence, telling yourself, "Don't do that, that's bad," actually can backfire. And we can talk about the psychology if that's interesting of why abstinence backfires. But a much healthier technique is not to tell yourself no. It's to tell yourself not yet. (00:19:57): You're not saying no, you're saying not yet. And so, you can do just about anything for 10 minutes. So, what I tell myself is, "Okay, I'm just going to wait 10 minutes before I check email, before I scroll social media, before I Google something that is just trying to procrastinate doing the work." I can do that. I'm a grown man. I can do whatever I want. I can do that in 10 minutes. And so, for those 10 minutes, all I have to do is either get back to the task at hand, get back to writing, or surf the urge, which is simply experiencing that sensation, acknowledging, "You know what? This is hard work. That's okay. That's why I'm feeling frustrated. That's why I'm feeling bored. That's why I'm feeling anxious. That's why I have this cold start around I don't really want to do this work because it's difficult." (00:20:34): So, what I do is I take a deep breath and I repeat a mantra that I made up for myself. You can make up your own mantra. My personal mantra whenever I feel this internal trigger is I remind myself this. I say, "This is what it feels like to get better. This is what it feels like to get better." And just saying that for as long as I need to until that emotion crests and subsides and then get back to work. What you'll find nine times out of 10 is that by the time those 10 minutes are up, you will have forgotten about that sensation. You'll be right back at the task at hand. And so, that's what's called the 10-minute rule. And of course what you're doing over time is that the 10-minute rule can become the 12-minute rule, can become the 20-minute rule, and most importantly, you are proving to yourself that you have agency that you said you were going to focus on a task and you did. That's the most important part. (00:21:22): The flip that we need to change in people's minds is this ridiculous belief that technology is hijacking our brains. There's nothing we can do about distraction that our focus is being stolen. It's not being stolen, we're giving it away. And so, what we need to do is to empower ourselves by showing ourselves in practice as well as in theory that we can postpone that distraction when we say we will.
turns.zh:
天哪，这太对了。确实如此，可我还没想出怎么让事情突然变得容易。每个字都很难敲出来，但我必须把它做好，而且我也乐在其中。完成后会很有成就感。但过程确实艰难。不过一旦有所发现、创造出有用的成果，那就乐趣无穷了。但实际做事的过程实在太难了。所以，我现在是这么做的。每次我想要去做别的事——这种情况随时都会发生——我就拿出计时器，拿出手机说：“设置10分钟计时。”然后放下手机，在这10分钟里，我随时准备回归手头任务，或者做个所谓的“冲动管理”。（00:19:12）：冲动管理的核心是承认这些情绪就像海浪。它们会涌起又退去。但我们对情绪的理解并非如此。我们大多数人认为情绪会一直存在。比如感到无聊，就觉得自己永远无聊；感到沮丧，就觉得永远沮丧，但事实并非如此。情绪就像海浪。所以你的任务是设定10分钟计时器，意识到自己几乎能在10分钟内完成任何事。关键不在于说不，而是说暂缓。（00:19:57）：你不是说不，而是说暂缓。所以10分钟内你能做任何事。我对自己说：“好的，我要等10分钟再查看邮件、刷社交媒体、谷歌搜索那些拖延工作的东西。”我能做到。我是个成年人了。我可以随心所欲。10分钟足够了。这10分钟里，我要么回归写作任务，要么冲动管理，也就是体验这种情绪，承认：“你知道吗？这工作真难。但没关系。这就是为什么我感到沮丧、无聊、焦虑。这就是为什么我对这项困难的工作毫无热情。”（00:20:34）：所以我深呼吸，重复我为自己制定的口头禅。你可以自己编造口头禅。我的口头禅是每当感觉到这种内在触发时，就提醒自己：“这就是变好的感觉。这就是变好的感觉。” 不断重复，直到情绪退去，再回归工作。九成情况下，10分钟一到，你就会忘记那种感觉，重新投入任务。这就是所谓的10分钟规则。当然，随着时间推移，10分钟可能变成12分钟、20分钟，最重要的是，你要证明自己有自控力，能专注于任务。这才是关键。（00:21:22）：我们需要改变的观念是，科技正在劫持我们的大脑。这是荒谬的信念。其实我们的注意力并没有被偷走。不是被偷走，而是我们自己放弃了。
把它放弃掉。所以，我们需要做的是通过实践和理论来证明自己，当我们说要延迟分心之事时，我们确实能够做到。这就是自我赋能的过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I like about this is one, it's kind of like the Pomodoro technique, but it's shorter. The 10 minutes I think is a really clever tweak versus 20 minutes, which a lot of people recommend. And then I guess a couple of follow-up questions. Do you do this one time in the morning and then not come back to it? Is this like a jump start for the day and then you start... If I start a thing like this, it won't be 10 minutes, it'll be like an hour because I'm like, "Okay, I did the hard thing, I'm into it. I'm just going to keep working." So, is this like a jump start for the morning or do you come back to this throughout the day?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个方法的原因有两点：首先，它有点类似番茄钟工作法，但时间更短。我认为10分钟的时长比很多人推荐的20分钟更明智。其次，我想问几个后续问题：你是一天只用一次吗？它是开启一天的动力源泉，还是你会全天反复回顾？比如我要是开始做这件事，就会持续一个小时而不是10分钟，因为我会想：“好吧，我已经完成了最难的部分，现在要继续下去。”所以，这到底是早晨的启动仪式，还是全天随时回顾？

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: So, you can do it whenever you find yourself slipping off track. And so, the Pomodoro is a version of this. I don't think it's complete enough because Pomodoro just said, "Set the timer, do it." Okay, fine. And that's great if it works for you. By the way, anything I'm saying right now, if the thing is working for you, if your life is awesome and you're doing what you said you're going to do, maybe this isn't the podcast. Maybe my book isn't the book for you, right? I'm talking to the people who, for whatever reason, you know you're capable of more, you know you're drifting off track. Maybe if like me, you said you were going to exercise but you didn't or you said you're going to eat right, but you don't. You said you were going to work on that big task, but you procrastinate. That's really who I was and that's who I wrote this book for. (00:22:49): And so, you can use that technique whenever you get distracted. It's not the whole picture. So, it's super important. Remember we talked about those four steps. This is just step number one. There's about a dozen different things you can do. Maybe this particular 10-minute rule doesn't work for you, doesn't work for everyone. There might be other techniques you use. So, there's dozens of different techniques just about this step around mastering internal triggers. But the next step to answer your question of well, how long do I go for? Do I do it for an hour? If now, I'm in the zone? And my answer is emphatically no. You don't go as long as you think you can. What you want to do, and this is step number two, is you're making time for traction by turning your values into time, which means you are going to make a time box schedule because you cannot call something a distraction unless you know what it distracted you from. (00:23:39): I'll say that again. You can't call something a distraction unless you know what it distracted you from. So, for me, at least, when I would succumb to, "Oh, let me just check email for a quick minute, let me just see what's happening on Twitter for a quick minute," part of that was because I would justify to myself, "Well, this is a work-related task. I got to do it sometime," and there wasn't a specific time to do it on my calendar, so I would keep thinking, "Well, I got to do it sometime. Might as well just do it now." And that's a huge mistake because if you can't look at your calendar and say, "Oh, that's traction." Okay, check email, write the blog post, post the podcast, go on social media. If that's not what's written in your calendar, if it's not there, it's a distraction. And so, it's not just work-related stuff. I literally have time in my calendar, spend time with my daughter, go on social media, watch Netflix. It's in my calendar. So now, I took what was previously distraction and I turned it into traction by putting it on my schedule.
turns.zh: 所以，当你发现自己偏离轨道时，随时都可以用这个方法。番茄钟工作法也是类似的模式。但我觉得它不够完善，因为番茄钟只说：“设置计时器，然后开始做事。”好吧，如果这对你有效，那当然不错。不过说实话，我现在所说的这些，如果事情对你有效，如果你的生活一帆风顺，你能按计划行事，那或许这个播客不适合你，也许我的书也不适合你，对吧？我是在和那些因为各种原因觉得自己能做得更好、却总在偏离轨道的人交流。比如我曾说过要锻炼却没做到，要合理饮食却没做到，要处理重要任务却拖拖拉拉。这就是我过去的自己，也是我写这本书的初衷。（00:22:49）所以，每当你分心时，都可以用这个技巧。但这只是整体方案的一部分。记住我们之前讨论的四个步骤，这只是第一步。还有十几种不同的方法来掌握内在触发机制。但接下来要回答你的问题：我该坚持多久？一个小时？如果现在我正处于专注状态呢？我的答案是：绝对不要延长到你觉得自己能坚持的极限。你要做的是第二步——通过将价值观转化为时间来为行动腾出空间。也就是说，除非你清楚被什么事物分散了注意力，否则你没法称它为干扰。（00:23:39）我再强调一遍：除非你清楚被什么事物分散了注意力，否则你没法称它为干扰。对我来说，至少当我忍不住想“哦，就快速看看邮箱，再看看推特动态”时，部分原因是我会自我辩解：“这毕竟是工作任务，总得找时间处理啊。”但我的日程表上并没有专门安排时间，所以我就会一直想：“总得找时间处理，不如现在就做。”这是一个巨大的错误。因为如果你不能看看日程表然后说：“哦，这就是行动。”那就去查邮箱、写博客、发布播客、刷社交媒体。如果这些不在你的日程表上，那就是干扰。而这些干扰不只是工作相关的。我的日程表里明明白白地写着：陪女儿、刷社交媒体、看Netflix。这些都被列入了日程。所以现在，我把以前的干扰转化成了行动，写进了日程表里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you actually do this through the day you have, "I'm going to check Twitter during this time of the day, I'm going to hang out with my daughter during this time of the day."
turns.zh: 也就是说，你实际上是根据自己每天的时间安排来规划行程的："我打算在一天中的这个时段查看推特，我打算在一天中的这个时段陪女儿玩耍。"

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Exactly. And you're adjusting it never in the day. So, you never want to do that. You always want to make sure you're doing it the day before. And so, what I do once a week, Sunday evenings, it takes me maybe 10 minutes a week. 8:00 P.M., I sit down, I look at my schedule for the week ahead and I ask myself, "Does this schedule reflect my values?" What are values? Values are attributes of the person you want to become. I'll say it again. Values are attributes of the person you want to become. So, there's three life domains, you, your relationships, and finally your work. So, what you got to do is you look at your calendar for the week ahead and you ask yourself, "How would the person I want to become spend time taking care of themselves?" That's the you domain. If you can't take care of yourself, you can't take care of others, you can't make the world a better place. (00:25:26): So then, you put in your calendar how you want to take care of yourself. What might that include? Well, time for rest. We all know how important sleep is, but I used to yell at my daughter and say, "Oh, it's your bedtime. You got to get to bed." And then one day she said to me, "Daddy, do you have a bedtime?" She was absolutely right. I was a hypocrite because I know how important sleep is and I didn't have a bedtime. Now, I have a bedtime. It's in my schedule. Then put in time for whatever else is important to you. Is reading important to you? Is prayer important to you? Is meditation, is exercise, is video games, is that important to you? Great. Whatever's important to you according to your values, put it in your schedule. Then you're going to put your relationships in. So, don't let the relationships in your life get whatever scraps of time are left over. (00:26:08): Put time in your schedule for your significant other, for your kids, for your buddies. How many of us are trapped in this loneliness epidemic because we don't make time for our closest relationships, including adult friendships? Don't let those wither away. Put time in your schedule for those, as well. We know that most friendships, they don't die in some big blowout. Relationships starve to death because we don't invest in them. Put time in your schedule for those relationships. We can talk about how to do that, as well. Then finally, the work domain involves two kinds of work. We have what's called reactive work and reflective work. Reactive work, reacting to notifications, reacting to emails, reacting to taps on the shoulder from your colleagues. That's going to be part of everybody's day. I get that, but don't let that be your entire day because what most people do, they habituate into not wanting to think. (00:26:56): They don't want to think what's important. "So, just let me look at my email inbox. My email inbox will tell me what to do. What's really important for my business? That's really hard. I don't really want to think about that. I'll look at my to-do list and I'll start ticking off easy tasks to do that make me feel productive." That's terrible. What you want to do instead is to book time in your schedule for this reflective work time, which is where you do the kind of work that requires you to work without distraction. Planning, strategizing, thinking, for god's sakes, can only be done without distraction. So, that fills up your calendar, as well. And what you're going to find, that there's never enough time for everything, which is good because what this forces you to do, and this is one of the main reasons why to-do lists suck, is because to-do lists have no constraints. (00:27:38): You can always add more to a to-do list. You can always add more, but here's what happens. This is what happened to me. I would get home from work. I have a very busy day and I'd look at my to-do list and it's a hundred items long and I think, "Wow, I've been working real hard all day and look at all this stuff I still didn't do. Loser." And so, day after day, week after week, month after month, I was reinforcing this self-image as someone who doesn't know how to manage their time. And then I started saying stupid stuff like, "Oh, maybe I'm no good at time management. Maybe I have undiagnosed ADHD. Maybe there's something wrong with me." There's nothing wrong with me. There's something wrong with this very stupid to-do list method, which doesn't force you to understand that there are trade-offs that you have to prioritize properly and that can only be done with constraints and that constraints come from your calendar. (00:28:23): So, you're turning your values into time by making time for traction and having this calendar and then, only then you can look at your calendar and say, "Ah, whatever it is I plan to do, that's traction. Everything else is distraction."
turns.zh:
确实如此。而且你绝不能在白天调整日程。所以你永远不该这么做。你得确保在前一天就把事情安排妥当。我每周日晚上都会花10分钟左右的时间做这件事。晚上8点，我会坐下来，查看接下来一周的日程安排，然后问自己："这份日程是否符合我的价值观？"什么是价值观？价值观是我们想成为的人所具备的特质。我再强调一遍，价值观是我们想成为的人所具备的特质。人生有三个领域：自我、人际关系和工作。因此，你需要在日程表中规划如何关爱自己。这属于自我领域。如果连自己都照顾不周，就无法关爱他人，也无法让世界变得更美好。（00:25:26）那么，如何在日程中安排关爱自己的时间呢？比如，休息时间。我们都知道睡眠的重要性，但我过去常常对女儿吼道："该睡觉了！"有一天她反问我："爸爸，你自己有睡觉时间吗？"她说得太对了。我是个伪君子，因为我明明知道睡眠的重要性，却没有自己的固定睡眠时间。现在我有了。我把它写进日程表。接下来是人际关系领域。别让生活中的关系成为被剩余时间填补的空白。（00:26:08）为伴侣、孩子、好友留出专属时间。多少人深陷孤独危机，就是因为我们不肯为最亲近的关系投入时间。别让这些情谊逐渐消逝。同样，为这些关系留出时间。我们可以探讨具体方法。最后，工作领域分为两种类型：被动式工作和主动式工作。被动式工作包括回复通知、处理邮件、应付同事的打扰。这些都是日常必做之事，我理解这些需求，但别让它们占据你的一整天。大多数人陷入习惯性思维，逃避深层思考。（00:26:56）他们说："就看看邮箱吧，邮箱会告诉我该做什么。业务重点太难了，不想动脑。看看待办清单，勾选几个简单任务，就觉得高效了。"这种做法很糟糕。你需要在日程中预留主动式工作时间，即专注于无干扰环境下的深度思考：规划、战略制定、深度思考。这些工作必须在无干扰状态下完成。所以，日程表也会被填满。你会发现时间永远不够用，但这恰恰是件好事，因为这迫使你正视一个现实——待办清单之所以失败，核心原因在于缺乏约束力。
（00:27:38）：你随时都可以在待办清单上添加更多任务。确实能添加，但问题在于：我曾有过这样的经历。下班回家后，我会审视自己的待办清单，发现上面有上百项任务。我就会想：“哇，我一整天都忙得不可开交，可看看这些还没完成的任务，真是太失败了。” 于是日复一日，周复一周，月复一月，我不断强化着自己是个不善于管理时间的人的自我认知。后来我甚至开始胡思乱想：“或许我不擅长时间管理？或许我患有未确诊的多动症？或许我本身就存在问题？” 但其实问题不在我，而是在于那份极其愚蠢的待办清单方法。它从不迫使你认识到：管理时间需要权衡取舍，而这种取舍只有在时间约束下才能合理进行——而时间约束恰恰来自你的日程表。  
（00:28:23）：所以，你要先把自己的价值观转化为时间资源，为重要任务腾出时间，再借助日程表规划日程。这样一来，你才能审视日程表时清晰分辨："无论我计划做什么，这都是推进工作的关键任务，其余皆为干扰。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to share a couple things that worked for me that are very much along these lines. One is booking. I call it deep work time within the day. This was the only thing I had in the calendar, so I didn't do the other things, which I think would've been really helpful, but I had a, I called it deep work time. I will slap you if you book anything over this meeting.
turns.zh: 我想分享几个对我有效的做法，它们都大致遵循了上述思路。其一是预留专注时间。我把这段时间称为一天中的深度工作时段。这是我日程表上唯一安排好的事项，所以其他可能很有帮助的事我都顾不上了，但我始终坚持这段深度工作时间。要是有人在这场会议之后再安排任何事，我非扇他不可。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: I love it.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这个做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I did that every Monday morning, Wednesday morning, and Friday sometime, and on that...
turns.zh: 我每周一上午、周三上午，还有周五的某个时段都会这样做。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Who was slapping you?
turns.zh: 谁会扇你？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I would be slapping the person that booked time over that slot and nobody can...
turns.zh: 我会扇预订了这段专注时间的人，而且谁都不能……

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Okay, got it.
turns.zh: 好的，我明白了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I don't know if that's allowed these days. I don't know how this...
turns.zh: 我不知道现在这样做是否被允许。我不知道该怎么做……

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Depends who you're booking with, I guess.
turns.zh: 这取决于你预订的是谁，我猜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, make it a little less aggressive maybe. But that worked a ton. It was like a two- or three-hour block of deep work time and that made a big dent in my ability to have time to focus because people weren't booking me as a PM.
turns.zh: 是啊，或许可以稍微不那么强硬一点。但那招确实很管用。我能有两个或三个小时的深度工作时间，这大大提升了我专注工作的能力，因为人们不再预订我的项目经理服务了。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Yeah, I love it. And by the way, I want to hear more of these, but that illustrates a really good point that when the stakes are high enough, I hear people a lot of times saying, "I just can't find the time to focus and I can't get this done and it's impossible these days." And then I say, "Well, let's make a little wager here." Let's say, I get this around physical fitness a lot or somebody says, "Oh, I want to be an author. How do I do that? How do I write the book? I can't seem to find the time." And they constantly say why They can't, they can't, they can't. "There's this constraint. My boss wants this. My kids want that." They have every kind of excuse. And then I say, "Okay, let's say that if you don't work out, 8:00 A.M. Monday morning, if you don't work out, you're going to have to pay me $10,000. Are you going to do it? Are you going to work out?" (00:30:03): "Well, of course, I'm going to work out. Easily. Yes, of course." Okay, so we've established you can. Now, we're just negotiating the price. So, this has to do with step four around making pacts, making what's called a pre-commitment, and one of them is a price pact. This is how I got in shape. I used to be clinically obese. Today, I'm in the best shape of my life, partially because I use these pacts. Now, the important thing is you have to do this last. If you don't figure out the internal triggers, most importantly, if you don't make time for traction in your schedule, if you don't hack back the external triggers, this fourth step won't work. But as the last line of defense, it's incredibly impactful and we can talk about how to do that, as well.
turns.zh: 是啊，我喜欢这样。顺便说一句，我想听更多这样的例子，但这确实说明了一个很重要的观点：当压力足够大时，人们常说：“我就是找不到时间专注，事情做不完，现在太难了。” 然后我会说：“那我们来打个赌吧。” 比如，我经常谈到健身话题，或者有人说：“我想成为作家，该怎么做？怎么写书？我总找不到时间。” 他们总是找借口，比如“老板有要求”，“孩子需要照顾”等等。然后我会说：“好吧，如果你周一早上8点不锻炼，就得给我1万美元。你能做到吗？” （00:30:03）：“嗯，当然能做到。没问题。”好，我们确定你能做到。现在就来协商价格。这涉及到第四步——达成协议，所谓的预先承诺，其中之一就是价格协议。这就是我如何塑形的。我曾经严重肥胖。如今，我状态最佳，部分原因就是靠这些协议。关键是，你得把这步放在最后。如果你不找出内在触发因素，最重要的是，如果你不为日程安排腾出时间，不消除外部干扰因素，第四步就行不通。但作为最后的防线，它效果惊人，我们可以探讨如何做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I heard the all-in guys did this to lose weight. I think Sax and Jason did a pact, too. I think it was a lot of money, a hundred thousand dollars or something wild for...
turns.zh: 我听说那些全力以赴的人就是用这个方法减肥的。我记得Sax和Jason也达成了协议。他们下了很大赌注，比如十万美元之类的。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Oh, that's awesome. Actually, that's what I used to finish this book, as well. Maybe they read my book, I wonder, because I talked about this exact situation.
turns.zh: 哦，太棒了。实际上，我写这本书时也是用了这个方法。也许他们读了我的书，我想知道，因为我书里就讲了这种情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You hit it. It sounds like. You made it.
turns.zh: 你说到点子上了。听起来你成功了。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: I did? Yeah.
turns.zh: 我这么做了？对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another trick I'll share that I found useful around the to-do list. So, I used to-do lists, but I've learned that I can't just let them grow is when I had a regular job. I wrote it down in a notebook and every morning, I rewrote the to-do list so that it reminded me like, "Okay, I've copied this thing 10 times now. I'm not going to do it. I'm just going to push it out." So, that act of just rethinking about it every day was really impactful. But that works for people that are okay with an analog to-do list. If it's digital, that doesn't go away.
turns.zh: 接下来我要分享一个在待办事项清单方面我发现很有用的技巧。以前我也用过待办事项清单，但后来发现当我有固定工作时，光是让它们堆积起来是不行的。我会把任务写在笔记本上，每天早上重新整理清单，这样能提醒自己：“好吧，这个任务我已经复写了十遍了，还是不去执行。我就把它先放一放吧。” 所以，每天重新审视待办事项这个做法真的很有效。但这种方法只适用于能接受纸质待办清单的人。如果是数字化的清单，问题依然存在。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: So, I just want to clarify, there's nothing wrong with taking things out of your brain and putting them on a piece of paper. That's wonderful, but that's step one. And so, the big mistake that people make is they put stuff on their to-do list and then they wake up in the morning and what are they supposed to do? "Well, I'll do whatever's on my to-do list." And so, what they tend to do is the easy stuff. I've known people, I hate to tell you, I used to do this myself, too. I would do a task and then forget to put it on my to-do list. So, I would go back in and write it on my to-do list just so I could check off the box. How messed up is that? It's ridiculous. And I think this is something that I think really does need to change is that we have this culture where checking stuff off your list is our little emotional reward, right? (00:32:12): But that's ridiculous. We need to stop measuring ourselves by how many cute little boxes we check off. And rather, a much more important metric is not, "Did I finish the task?" I don't want you to track, "Did I finish?" That's not the important part, but people are probably scratching their heads. What do you mean? Isn't it all about finishing what I have to do? No, the important part is figuring out your productivity. It's figuring out how efficient you are at using your time. So, a much more beneficial metric to track is not, "Did I check off the box? Did I finish?" Rather, it's, "Did I do what I said I was going to do for as long as I said I would without distraction?" I'll say it again. "Did I do what I said I was going to do for as long as I said I would without distraction?" (00:32:53): Because that is the only way to understand how long things take you. The problem with to-do lists is that there is no feedback loop, there's no feedback mechanism. How long do things take you? So, this is why you have what's called the planning fallacy with people who use to-do lists, which says that on average, studies have found that tasks take people three times longer to finish than they estimate. Why does that happen? Because when you say, "Okay, here's that thing on the to-do list. I'm going to work on that and see how long it takes me to get it done." So, you work on it for five minutes and then you get an email and then you get a notification and then you start talking to one of your colleagues and you never actually track how long that thing took you to finish, as opposed to when you say, "Look, I'm going to work on that task for as long as I said I would, but without distraction. That's it. That's all I'm going to do." (00:33:39): What you now have is a metric of how far you got. So, I worked on that presentation, it needs to be 30 slides long, and I worked on it for 30 minutes and I finished two slides. Okay, great. Well now, I know that I need 10 more of those time boxes to finish the entire task. And this is why it turns out that people who measure themselves the way I espouse of people who say, "I'm just going to measure myself based on, did I do what I said I was going to do for as long as I said I would without distraction regardless of whether I finished," the kicker here is they actually finish more. They get more done than the to-do list people because now, they understand how long things take them to finish and they can appropriately time that as opposed to what most of us did. (00:34:20): What I used to do before I wrote Indistractable was procrastinate, procrastinate, procrastinate. "Oh crap, I got to get this done. The deadline's here, so I'm going to work all night to finish it," and of course, that's not when you do your best work and it's very stressful.
turns.zh:
好，我想先澄清一下，把事情从大脑中提取出来写在纸上并没有什么错。这很棒，但这只是第一步。人们常犯的一个大错误是，把任务列入待办清单后，第二天早上醒来却不知道该做什么。"好吧，我得把待办清单上的事都做完。"结果他们往往只做那些简单的事。我认识一些人，说实话我自己也曾这样做过。我会完成一项任务，却忘了把它加到待办清单上。于是我又回去把它写上去，就为了能划掉那个框。这多糟糕啊？简直荒谬。我认为真正需要改变的是，我们的文化把完成待办清单上的任务当作一种小小的情感奖励，对吧？（00:32:12）但这太荒谬了。我们不该用划掉清单上的框来衡量自己，而是应该关注一个更重要的指标——不是“我完成了任务吗？”而是“我按照计划用心完成了任务吗？”人们可能觉得奇怪，这话什么意思？难道完成任务不重要吗？不重要，重要的是要评估自己的效率。衡量效率的标准不应该是完成了任务，而是“我按照计划专心完成了任务吗？”（00:32:53）因为这才是理解任务耗时长短的唯一方法。待办清单的问题在于缺乏反馈机制。任务实际需要多长时间？因此使用待办清单的人常犯“规划谬误”——研究发现，人们完成任务的时间往往比预估的多三倍。为什么会这样？因为当你说“好，我要处理待办清单上的这个任务，看看需要多久。”结果你工作五分钟后收到邮件、通知，又和同事聊天，却从不记录完成时间。而当你说“好，我要按照计划专心完成任务，不受干扰，就这样。”你就能准确衡量进度了。比如制作演示文稿，需要30张幻灯片，我工作30分钟完成两张。好的，我知道还需要10个时间框才能完成整个任务。这就是为什么按照我所倡导的方式衡量自己的人——他们说“我只需根据是否按照计划专心完成任务来评价自己，而不论是否完成”——结果他们完成得更多。比待办清单用户效率高得多，因为他们能准确规划时间，而不是像我们大多数人那样拖拖拉拉。（00:34:20）在写《不分心》之前，我一直在拖延。“哦糟糕，得完成这个任务了。截止日期快到了，所以我要通宵完成。”结果
当然，那可不是你能发挥出最佳工作状态的时候，而且压力还特别大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Since you mentioned deadlines, do you have any advice lessons on that as a tool to get things done?
turns.zh: 既然你提到了截止日期，那你有没有关于利用截止日期来完成任务的建议？

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: What we find is that people who are very deadline motivated, they do finish what they say they're going to do, but of course, the quality is crap. They're typically getting by by the skin of their teeth, and I did this all the time. This is my entire college career and my MBA at Stanford career was waiting, waiting, waiting, and then finishing at the last moment. And I could do well enough, but of course, I could do so much better if I worked without distraction. And so, it wasn't until, and we all know this basically, right? We know that putting in a little bit of diligent effort, a little bit at a time with plenty of lead time is going to give us a much better result than cramming at the last minute. But the reason people don't do this is because they don't understand how important it is, one, to manage those internal triggers. (00:35:22): If you're constantly thinking, "Ugh, that project is going to suck. I don't really want to work on it. I don't want to make those sales calls. I don't want to make that presentation. I don't want to do that thing that feels uncomfortable," and you don't have the tools to deal with that discomfort, you're always going to procrastinate because fundamentally, procrastination is an emotion regulation problem. It's not a character flaw. There's nothing wrong with you, you're not broken. It's just that you don't have the tools to deal with emotional discomfort and that's the part that everybody skips over. So, we don't want to talk about these uncomfortable feelings, but that's where it has to start. And then, the part that people don't do is actually planning out not the task itself, but the time to work on the task without distraction. That's the part that if you can implement that step two that I talked about of making time for traction, that becomes a game changer.
turns.zh: 我们发现，那些非常受截止日期驱使的人确实能完成他们承诺要做的事，但当然，质量往往很差。他们通常是勉强应付，我自己在大学和斯坦福商学院的整个经历都是这样——一直在等待，等待，等待，最后在最后一刻才完成任务。虽然结果还算过得去，但如果没有干扰的话，我本可以做得更好。直到现在，我们都知道这个道理，对吧？我们知道提前一点努力，分阶段处理并预留充足时间，总比临时抱佛脚效果好得多。但人们不这么做的原因是他们不明白这有多重要，首先是管理内部触发因素。（00:35:22）如果你总在想：“啊，这个项目肯定很糟糕。我真不想做它。我不想打那些销售电话。我不想做那个让我不舒服的演示。”而你又没有应对这种不适的工具，那你就会一直拖延，因为本质上，拖延是一个情绪调节的问题。这不是性格缺陷。你没有毛病，只是你没有应对情绪不适的工具，而这正是人们忽视的部分。所以，我们不想谈论这些不舒服的感觉，但这正是问题的根源。然后，人们没有做的是规划任务本身，而是规划在没有干扰的情况下完成任务的时间。如果你能实施我提到的第二步——为推进任务腾出时间，那就会产生巨大的改变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, I've tried things like this where it's here throughout the day, I'm going to try this, I'm going to do this and this, and I just don't end up doing it. Things come up or I just get distracted. I'm like, whatever. I guess one question is how often do you find yourself doing the things you set out in your calendar? And then two, any other advice for actually staying on track and doing things you set out to?
turns.zh: 所以，我尝试过这样的方法：一整天都把事情列在清单上，然后尝试去做这些事，但最后还是没做成。总有突发情况或者我被分心了。我就会想，管他呢。我有个问题，你觉得你能按时完成日历上安排的任务吗？然后，第二个问题，有什么保持正轨、完成既定任务的其他建议吗？

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Okay, so number one, did you have tools in place to deal with the discomfort? What did you do when you didn't feel it?
turns.zh: 好的，首先，你有没有应对不适感的工具？当你感觉不到不适时，你会怎么做？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did not. I did not have that surfing the wave and the ten-minute trick, and I'm curious if there's other tricks in that bucket actually, but no, I did not.
turns.zh: 我没有。我没有那种“顺势而为”和“十分钟技巧”，我很好奇是否还有其他类似的方法，但没有，我没有。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Absolutely. Yeah. So, that's the most important thing and that is the most important section. That's why I put it at the front of the book because again, procrastination is an emotion regulation problem, and I think this is fascinating. Personally, I really wanted to dive deep and not only understand why do we not do what we say we're going to do, but why do we do anything and everything? What is the seat of human motivation? And I think I didn't understand it properly. I think most people don't understand motivation properly. Doesn't that blow your mind? If you think about it, "I know what to do. I agree, this is what needs to get done. I just don't do it." Isn't that ridiculous? And by the way, this is not a new problem. Plato, 2500 years ago, the Greek philosopher talked about this very same problem. 2500 years before the internet, before social media, before all these things that we think are so distracting online, the Greek philosopher has had the same exact problem. (00:37:27): This is part of the human condition. It is part of our DNA that we constantly get distracted. But to me, that's a fascinating mystery. Why is that? Well, if you look at the deeper question of why do we do anything and everything, the seat of human motivation most people think is about carrots and sticks. If you ask people, why do we do what we do? It's about the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain. Jeremy Bentham said something similar to this. Sigmund Freud called it the pleasure principle. Neurologically speaking, it's not true. It's not true. It's not about the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain. It's not about carrots and sticks, but in fact, the carrot is the stick, okay? This is where I want to give you that matrix-like... Remember that scene, the Matrix, where there's that kid with a spoon and the spoon starts bending and the kid says, "Imagine there is no spoon," right?
turns.zh: 没错。是的。所以，这是最重要的事情，也是最重要的章节。这就是为什么我把它放在书的开头，因为拖延其实是一个情绪调节问题，我觉得这非常有趣。就我个人而言，我真的很想深入探讨这个问题——不仅要理解为什么我们做不到自己说要做的事，还要理解我们为什么会做任何事？人类动机的根源在哪里？我觉得我之前并没有真正理解它。我认为大多数人对动机都理解得不够。这难道不令人惊讶吗？想想看，“我知道该做什么。我也认同这件事需要完成，但我就是不去做。”这不是很荒谬吗？顺便说一句，这可不是个新问题。2500年前，希腊哲学家柏拉图就谈到了同样的问题。早在互联网、社交媒体、这些我们认为会让人分心的东西出现之前，希腊哲学家就已经面临着同样的问题了。（00:37:27）这是人类的本性特征。我们天生就容易分心。但对我来说，这是一个非常迷人的谜团。为什么会这样？如果你深入探讨我们为什么会做任何事这个更深层的问题，大多数人认为人类动机的根源在于奖惩机制。如果你问人们为什么会做某件事，他们会说这是为了追求快乐，避免痛苦。杰里米·边沁也提过类似观点。西格蒙德·弗洛伊德称之为快乐原则。从神经学角度来看，这种说法并不正确。关键不在于追求快乐、避免痛苦，也不在于奖惩机制。事实上，奖惩机制本身就是动力的来源。好吧，我想给你们讲讲类似矩阵的……还记得《黑客帝国》里的那个场景吗？一个孩子用勺子弯曲勺子，然后孩子说：“想象一下勺子不存在。”对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Well, the carrot is the stick. What do I mean by that? We know that the only reason we do everything in anything from a neurological perspective is not about the pursuit of pleasure. It is all about the desire to escape discomfort. Everything you do, even the pursuit of pleasurable sensations, the carrot is the stick, because even wanting to feel good, craving, lusting, desire, hunger, that desire for something that feels good is itself psychologically destabilizing. The carrot is the stick. So, what that means, I think that's incredibly empowering because what that means is that whenever we don't do something, whenever we procrastinate, it's just a feeling. It's all it is. It's just a feeling. And so, when we learn those tools, it doesn't mean where I think people start intellectualizing it and thinking, "There must be something broken with me. Maybe you need a pill, maybe you need a treatment." (00:39:07): Chances are there's a ninety-nine percent chance, there's nothing wrong with you. It's simply that you don't have these tools. So, that's where we have to start, is absolutely understanding and applying these techniques so that when you feel that discomfort, you use that discomfort. What I found in my research writing this book is that high performers in every industry, business, the arts, sports, high performers, they feel the same internal triggers. They also feel lonely. They also feel bored. They also feel stressed. They also feel anxious, but they use that discomfort like a rocket fuel to propel them towards traction. Whereas what distractable people do, as soon as they feel uncomfortable, as soon as they feel bored, as soon as they feel lonesome, as soon as soon as they feel indecisive or stressed, boom, they're escaping it with a drink, with a click, with something to take their mind off of that discomfort. So, that has to be step number one.
turns.zh: 嗯，胡萝卜加大棒的策略。我这么说是什么意思呢？我们知道，从神经学角度来看，我们做任何事的唯一动机都不是为了追求快乐，而是为了逃避不适感。你所做的每一件事，即便是在追求愉悦感时，也是胡萝卜加大棒，因为即使想感觉良好、渴望、欲望、饥求、对美好事物的渴望本身也会导致心理不稳定。胡萝卜加大棒。所以，我认为这非常有力量，因为这意味着每当我们不做某件事，每当我们拖延时，那只是一种感觉。仅此而已。一种感觉。当我们掌握了这些技巧后，人们往往不会陷入自我否定，认为自己有问题——或许需要服药，或许需要治疗。（00:39:07）：很可能99%的情况下，你没有任何问题。只不过你没有掌握这些技巧。所以，我们必须从这里开始，彻底理解并应用这些技巧，这样当你感受到不适感时，就利用这种不适感。通过我的研究和写作，我发现每个行业、每个领域的优秀者——商业、艺术、体育——都会感受到同样的内在触发。他们也会感到孤独、无聊、压力重重、焦虑不安，但他们会把这种不适感当作火箭燃料，推动自己前进。而那些容易分心的人，一旦感到不适、无聊、孤独、犹豫不决或压力重重，就立刻用一杯饮料、一次点击、任何能转移注意力的事物来逃避它。所以，这必须是第一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is fascinating. Basically, distraction is an emotional regulation problem. It's the way you put it. What else works in helping you manage that discomfort? We've talked about this ten-minute trick, the timer, the surfing of the urge. What else is in that bucket of things I could try when I'm just like, "Nah, I'm just going to go check Twitter. I need to work on this thing, right now."
turns.zh: 这真是令人着迷。基本上，分心就是情绪调节的问题。正如你所说。还有什么方法能帮助我们应对这种不适感？我们已经谈到了十分钟技巧、计时器、冲动控制等方法。当我们想“算了，还是去看看推特吧。我现在就得处理这件事”时，还能尝试哪些方法？

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Yeah, so there's a bunch of different techniques you can use there in terms of the internal triggers. We can get into some of the more nitty-gritty techniques. There's lots and lots of them. The most important thing here though is that once you have some in your toolkit that you want to try, let's say it's a ten-minute rule, it's surfing the urge, there's re-imagining the task, the temperament, all kinds of things that you can do. The next thing is to put it on your calendar, which we talked about briefly. So, let's say you say, "Okay, I've got that time when I..." What did you say that you want to do, that you check email instead?
turns.zh: 是的，针对这些内在触发因素，有很多不同的技巧。我们可以深入探讨一些更具体的技巧。技巧有很多，但最重要的是，一旦你掌握了某个想尝试的技巧，比如十分钟规则、冲动控制、重新构想任务、调整心态等各种方法，下一步就是把它写进日历里，我们之前也简要提过。比如，你说你有那个时间段，而你却在查看邮件？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Start on my newsletter post for the next week, or just continue.
turns.zh: 开始写下周的通讯文章，或者继续做其他事。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: To write it?
turns.zh: 是啊，写下来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, write it.
turns.zh: 对啊，写下来。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Okay. And did you have that in your calendar? That was part of the time punch-me-in-the-face-if-I-don't-do-it kind of thing?
turns.zh: 好的。你把它写进日历了吗？这就是那种“如果我不做，就抽自己耳光”的那种提醒吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was back when I had a regular job. These days, it's just, what I used to do is my first half of the day until 3:00 is just deep work time. I called it it's-time-to-build time, and then 3:00 beyond is meetings. So, it was actually a huge block of time of focus time, but it was not subdivided by the things I wanted to do throughout the day.
turns.zh: 当时我还有一份固定工作。如今，我每天的工作安排是这样的：上午9点到下午3点是深度工作时间，我称之为“专注时段”，而下午3点之后则要参加会议。所以，实际上这段时间本应是连续的专注时段，但却被我全天想做的事情分割得支离破碎。

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: I see. Okay. So, step two would be putting on your calendar, "I'm going to work on writing this newsletter for 30 minutes, 45 minutes, whatever amount of time." Make it whatever is reasonable for you based on how long you think you can do it. Put that on your schedule. Okay? Step number three is hack back the external triggers. So, did you find that when you said I was going to work on writing this newsletter, was there anything in your external environment that was pinging, dinging, kids, pets, spouse, anything like that?
turns.zh: 我明白了。好的，第二步是在日历上标注：“我要花30分钟、45分钟或任意时长来写这份时事通讯。” 根据你的实际情况合理设定时长。把这项任务加入日程安排。第三步是规避外部干扰。比如，当你决定专心写时事通讯时，外部环境是否会频繁发出提醒——孩子哭闹、宠物叫唤、配偶打扰之类的干扰因素？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that now that you say that, just that fact that only 10% of distractions are from that. So, it makes me, on the one hand, I recognize that most of the time, there's not a thing pulling me to Twitter, LinkedIn, or whatever. Most of the time, it's just like, that's probably something interesting going on. But there's definitely times when I see a little badge or my little phone gets a little push or yeah, my wife's with a kid in the distance. I'm like, "Oh, let's go check out what's happening there."
turns.zh: 很有意思的是，你刚说只有10%的干扰来自外部因素。这让我一方面意识到，大多数时候，真正吸引我去刷推特、刷领英的诱惑并不存在。大多数时候，可能只是觉得有趣的信息推送了。但确实有些时候，比如看到手机提示消息，或者妻子带着孩子在房间里，我就会想：“哦，过去看看有什么新鲜事。”

turns.speaker: Nir Eyal
turns.en: Yeah. So, that's where we want to hack back. So, the reason I use the term hack. To hack something is to gain unauthorized access. Someone hacks into your bank account or hacks into your database. We know that these technologies are gaining unauthorized access to our attention span when they're constantly pinging and dinging us. So, there's some very simple things you can do. Setting a schedule in advance so that your device turns off as it goes to do-not-disturb during certain times of the day or before you begin this task, before you start writing, you make sure to turn on do-not-disturb, so that there's nothing in your way. On my desktop, I have a do-not-disturb set from midnight to 11:59 all the time. It's constantly on do-not-disturb because I don't want these constant notifications disturbing me when I'm doing focus work. (00:42:52): So, making sure that that's on. When it comes to, many of us work from home today, so making sure that your family knows when the time is that you are indistractable. And I'll give you one tip. I know you have a baby at home, but soon, that baby is going to be a toddler. And so, one thing that we did in my household is that my wife went to Amazon and she got what we call the concentration crown. And the concentration crown is just this little wreath thing that she wears. It looks like a little princess thing. It has little LED lights. It lights up. There's a picture of it in the book. And when my daughter was only six years old, we told her, "Look, whenever mommy is wearing the concentration crown, that means that she can't be interrupted and she will be with you within 30 minutes." (00:43:37): So, her time block was always no more than 30 minutes. So, we said, "We will be with you within 30 minutes. Please don't interrupt unless you're bleeding. Okay? If you're bleeding, you can interrupt us, but unless you're bleeding," this is when my daughter was only six years old. She could find something to do. It's okay for kids to be bored time to time, but as long as mommy was wearing the concentration crown that told her, and by the way, me, as her significant other, as her husband, worked really, really well because I would always interrupt her and say, "Hey Julie, can I ask you this one thing?" And she was working on her computer, but I didn't know whether she was listening to a podcast or a video or doing work that needed concentration. So, hacking back those external triggers, making sure that they don't gain unauthorized access by interrupting the interruption, whether it's with your kids, your colleagues. (00:44:24): So, every copy of indistractable has this little pull-out piece of paper, this piece of card stock that you fold into thirds and you put on your computer monitor. Okay, it's this big red sign on your computer monitor that says, "I'm indistractable at the moment. Please come back later." Now you can say, "Well, why don't I just put on headphones and my colleagues will know I'm not to be interrupted?" Yeah, but then they think you're putzing around, playing video games or something on your machine, as opposed to if you say, "No, I'm doing focused work right now, please come back later," you're making it acceptable to not constantly be interrupted. You're making it okay culturally appropriate to work without distractions. So, those are just some ways that you can hack back those external triggers.

turns.zh: 是的，当然。那么，这就完美地引出了第四步。我们已经讨论了第一步——掌握内在触发因素，腾出时间推进进展，化解外部触发因素。刚刚我们还谈了第三步。第四步是通过协议防止分心。关于协议，有三种类型。第一种是价格协议，即设置某种财务惩罚机制来避免偏离轨道。这正是我们之前讨论的内容。你可以聊聊我如何利用这种方法首次成功减肥，或者完成一本书的写作。这就是价格协议。第二种是身份协议，影响力极大。这意味着你正在塑造个人身份。这源自宗教心理学——比如，自称穆斯林的人不会纠结是否要喝吉尼酒，因为虔诚的穆斯林不喝酒。（00:46:58）：又比如素食主义者或纯素主义者早上不会想：“嗯，我该不该吃培根三明治当早餐呢？” 不，他们就是素食主义者。这就是为什么这本书叫《不可分心》（Indistractable）。Indistractable的发音类似indestructible（坚不可摧）。它代表你的身份，代表你本身。那么，当有人说：“你知道吗？很抱歉我不能每30秒就查看每个通知提示。我是不可分心的。”或者“如果我们要一起用餐，如果我们要坐下来共进午餐，我希望这顿午餐没有任何干扰。所以，能不能把手机收起来？”这和那些宣称：“我有特定的饮食偏好”或者“我有特定的宗教着装要求”的人有何不同？（00:47:35）：不，也许这还不是常态。或许只有少数人会这样做。但我认为，要让整个世界变得不可分心，就必须有更多人展示出，当我们掌握了这些原则并将其融入个人身份时，我们能过上多么美好的生活。第三种协议叫做努力协议。这需要克服某种阻碍，需要付出某种努力才能分心。作为最后一道防线，这就是第四步——抵御干扰的最后防线。要确保你能像我们抵御外界干扰一样坚守内心。接下来我要讲个个人故事。我不知道这节目适不适合家庭收听。能不能稍微谈谈我的性生活？

turns.zh: 这事儿其实没听起来那么激动人心。我结婚已经22年了。我和妻子发现我们不再像从前那样亲密了。而这正是我开始写这本书的契机。问题部分在于，每天晚上我们上床后，她总是在摆弄iPhone，而我则在玩iPad。我们之所以缺乏亲密互动，是因为我们更热衷于玩手机而非彼此相伴。于是，我开始研究《专注力革命》（Indistractable）一书，了解到“努力契约”这个技巧。于是，我去五金店买了一个10美元的插座定时器。只要你插入设备，定时器就会在你设定的时间自动开启或关闭。（00:49:15）在我们家，一直到现在，每天晚上10点，互联网路由器都会自动关闭。这样做有什么效果呢？我们知道每天晚上10点，路由器都会断网。所以我的女儿、妻子和我都知道这一点。因为知道路由器要关机，我必须在那之前完成所有需要上网处理的事务。当然，我可以重新打开路由器，但这需要额外的精力。我现在采取的做法是，如果实在忍不住想玩手机，就用一点正念来克服这个坏习惯。现在我必须问自己："等等，我真的需要费那么大劲去重新插拔路由器吗？还是应该做我说要做的事——按时上床休息，或许还能和妻子亲密一下？"（00:50:05）这带来了天翻地覆的变化，老实说，莱尼，经过几年的坚持，这已经成了我们的日常习惯。我们都知道晚上10点该上床休息了。路由器会自动关机，现在我们甚至不需要这个定时器了，因为它已经融入了我们的生活。所以，这是任何人都可以使用的简单工具。另一个我几乎每天都在用的工具，我的女儿也用，那就是一款叫Forest的神奇应用。你知道Forest吗？

turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我现在要把你分享的所有内容都列出来，涵盖四个步骤，然后再深入探讨几个要点。以下是我的笔记。首先是设置十分钟计时器，告诉自己："我现在要专注做一件想做的事，十分钟内只做这件事。"在此期间，要克服冲动，尽管会感到不适，但要坚持下来，意识到这很困难。日程规划是你的核心方法，就是提前规划好每天要做的事。把待办事项列入日程表。说白了，你的待办事项就是你的日程表。（00:53:02）：你分享了各种协议想法，比如"如果我不做这件事，我就给你一大笔钱"。还有Wi-Fi关闭功能。好的。这些方法都可以转化为其他工具，比如Wi-Fi杀手设备、Forest应用、Focusmate产品。另外，你还提到了一些其他方法，比如全天开启免打扰模式，我也一直在这么做。让家人和重要联系人知道你的工作时间，这样他们就不会打扰你。或许还有专注力加冕器。
